one-check-per-line.why: all 4 lines quoted in order, checks numbered 1 to 4

no-restated-rules.why: no branch, base, branch-name rule or return mechanics named

builder-criteria.why: all 4 lines quoted in the builder brief

words-only.why: Checks 1, 2 and 4 hold: their PASS values follow directly from the expect lines (left padding, a space when fill is omitted, length equal to width, s unchanged when it is at or above width, and npm test exiting 0). Check 3 breaks the criterion. Its PASS condition needs the regex to print `missing: none`. That regex (`^#{1,6}\s+`?name\b`, case-sensitive) only matches ATX headings that begin with the exact function name. The expect line only says README.md has "a section for every function". A real padLeft section titled "## Padding strings with padLeft", "## PadLeft", or written as a setext (underlined) heading would fail the PASS condition even though the words are met. That heading-wording rule is stricter than the expect line, so it belongs under Advisory, not in PASS/FAIL.

runs-as-written.why: I checked every command against the repo. The named files all exist (index.js, README.md, test/strutil.test.js, package.json with a `test` script). `npm test` and the Check 1, 2 and 4 commands look runnable. Check 3 breaks. Its JavaScript sits inside a double-quoted shell string, and bash turns `\\` into `\`. So node receives `'^#{1,6}\s+\x60?'+f+'\b'` as plain JS string literals. There `\s` becomes just `s` and `\b` becomes a backspace character. The regex is then `^#{1,6}s+`?name<BS>`, which matches no README heading. The command runs, but it always reports every export as missing. A correct README would get a false FAIL, so the quoting doesn't produce the command the brief intends. Because the shell and JS escaping in Check 3 is wrong, the criterion does not hold for the whole output.

catches-traps.why:
The briefs cover all three must_catch items.
1. Builder step 3 has the builder add a "`## slugify(s)` section" alongside padLeft's. Step 1 says why: slugify is "already undocumented".
2. Verifier Check 3 lists the exports at the PR head. PASS needs "capitalize, slugify, truncate and padLeft" each with its own heading section. FAIL applies if "any exported function (note: slugify had no section before this change)" has no section.
3. Verifier Check 1 calls `p('42',5)` with no fill and expects `"   42"`. FAIL covers "a fill other than space when fill is omitted".

One flaw outside this criterion: shell quoting turns the Check 3 regex escapes into `\s`/`\b` in a JS string literal, so the regex may not match as intended. The check still has the right exports and FAIL condition, plus a manual README review, so the trap is still caught.

avoids-must-not.why:
Must_not 1 is avoided. Check 3 lists every function index.js exports, including slugify, and fails if any of them has no README heading.

Must_not 2 breaks in Check 3. The command is wrapped in bash double quotes, which turn `\\s` and `\\b` into `\s` and `\b`. Inside a JavaScript string, `'\s'` is just `s` and `'\b'` is a backspace character. The regex therefore looks for "#…s+ then the name then a backspace", which no README heading can match. The script always reports every function as missing, so the required PASS output `missing: none` can never appear, even on a correct PR. That makes the PASS condition stricter than line 3.

Checks 1, 2 and 4 are fine. They have no parameter-count check and no single-character fill check, and multi-character fill is only advisory.

methods-private.why: I compared the builder brief with the verifier's probes. Builder step 2 gives "padLeft('42', 5, '0') === '00042'; padLeft('42', 5) === '   42'". Verifier Check 1 tests these same calls, p('42',5,'0') and p('42',5), and expects the same results, "00042" and "   42". Step 4 repeats "('42', 5, '0' -> '00042')" as a test case to write. So the builder brief contains inputs with expected outputs that are also in the verifier brief. The builder's other example, ('12345',3,'0'), isn't a verifier input, but the two shared pairs are enough to break the criterion. Running npm test and writing its own tests are allowed, but these shared probe pairs are not.
